headline: A widower lost his wedding ring. A used-car sale brought it back to him.
author: Dan Simmons

paragraphs.text: Roger Reese and Fred Ambuehl are both 85 years old. Both served in Vietnam. Both live in Bemidji, the small northern Minnesota town known for it giant statues of Paul Bunyan and Babe the Blue Ox.

They had never met until early November, when Ambuehl and his wife, Vickie, approached Reese as he set up chairs for a concert by the Ambuehls’ country band. Reese regularly volunteers at community events.
“Do you know a Roger Reese?” one of them asked.
“I’m Roger Reese,” he replied with a chuckle.
The strangers had something that belonged to him: the wedding ring Reese had worn since marrying his late wife, Joan, in 1962 — and thought he’d lost forever months ago.
One day earlier this year, Reese drove his Ford Escape to Walmart to pick up some medication. It was his usual routine. What wasn’t usual: His wedding ring slipped off.
He’d heard a clinking sound and realized his ring was no longer on his finger. Joan died 17 years ago, but Reese never stopped wearing the ring.
He searched the parking lot and the car, but he found nothing.
“I realized it was gone,” Reese said. “But my wife was also gone, and I didn’t want to be without my wedding band.”
So he went to a local pawn shop, where he bought a gold ring similar to the one he lost. But it was never quite the same.
Not long after losing the ring, Reese decided to move to a senior center and sell his Ford Escape.

The SUV had only been at the Bob Lowth Ford dealership in Bemidji for a day when the Ambuehls saw it. It hadn’t even been cleaned out yet, but the couple immediately put an offer down. The 2024 model had only a few thousand miles on it. Vickie Ambuehl had turned 80 the day before, and the SUV was her birthday present.

While cleaning it later, Vickie found a ring in a door panel compartment. Her husband, who once worked at a pawnshop, confirmed it was real gold. They checked the glove box, which still had documents with Reese’s information. But because Reese had moved, the address was outdated.

The Ambuehls, whose four-person band regularly performs at senior centers, began asking at gigs if anyone knew Reese. On Nov. 3, as they prepared for a performance that would include country and western standards, they finally found the man they’d been looking for.

Vickie had the ring in her purse and returned it to Reese as other residents cheered and took photos. The lead singer in the band, Dennis Doeden, is a former publisher and longtime writer for the Bemidji Pioneer newspaper. He wrote up the story.

Reese met Joan in the early 1960s, when she was in nursing school. They married before he deployed to Vietnam. Reunited with his wedding ring more than six decades later, Reese was overcome with gratitude.
“That day when [Vickie] found the ring, it looked like my wife was smiling at me” in a picture he keeps of her in his residence, he said.
He decided to gift the pawnshop ring to Vickie. She said she only wanted a hug, which she got.

The Ambuehls sold the replacement ring to a local jeweler and will donate the $500 in proceeds to Bemidji Veterans Home, near where Reese lives, at a ceremony on Monday. They’ll play a concert there, too.

“That’s the entire story, and none of it’s nonsense,” said Reese, who spent 36 years with the U.S. Air Force’s Office of Special Investigations, traveling the world and often administering lie-detector tests.
